newsitem.title: CANADA: No rally in sight for slumping Canada dollar.
newsitem.headline: No rally in sight for slumping Canada dollar.

text.p: The Canadian dollar, which has lost almost four percent of its value against the U.S. dollar this year, shows no signs of rallying any time soon, economists said on Thursday.
The Canadian currency has dropped since January to 72.07 U.S. cents from 74.78 U.S. cents on concerns over domestic interest rates and political uncertainty.
Despite bright economic fundamentals, uncertainty over the Bank of Canada's timetable for an increase in interest rates has cast a pall over the currency, analysts said.

"I get the sense that until the Bank of Canada raises interest rates, the Canadian dollar will continue to be sluggish," said Steve Saldanha, an economist with Canada Trust Investment Management in Toronto.
"Markets are psychologically prepared for the (central) bank to move tomorrow or sometime in the next three months. As long as that is true, the Canada dollar rally isn't going to happen," he said.
The Bank of Canada's Governor Gordon Thiessen has come under increasing pressure to shift towared a less stimulative monetary policy.

So far, the central bank has lowered interest rates 11 times since the beginning of 1996, stimulating domestic economic growth and standing pat in the face of a small interest rate hike in the United States.
A 25 basis-point rise in U.S. rates by the Federal Reserve in March, hurt the Canadian dollar when the Bank of Canada opted not to follow with a similar rate rise of its own.

However, last month Thiessen made plain that he believed the Bank of Canada had the flexibility to move to a more neutral monetary policy, opening up the possibility that the Canadian central bank might match future Fed rate hikes.
The Canadian dollar rallied on Thiessen's comments, but soon fell back as markets began discounting the immediacy of such a move.
After a speech in Quebec City, Thiessen on Wednesday tried to talk up the dollar.

"We continue to believe that the underlying factors that affect the Canadian dollar over time are still ones that are going to lead to an upward trend in the Canadian dollar," Canada's top central banker told a news conference.
Dubious investors thought otherwise and sold the currency as it broke through technical support levels at 72.02 U.S. cents.
Also clouding the horizon is Canada's increasingly polarized political scene and the secessionist ambitions of separatists in mainly French-speaking Quebec to break away from the Canadian federation.

The election of a regionally divided parliament in Canada's June 2 federal election could mean another round of constitutional wrangling and ignite a third sovereignty referendum in Quebec, cautioned Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Nesbitt Burns in Toronto.
"Fundamentally, the currency should be a lot stronger, but we're not going to see a change as long as there is this political uncertainty regarding Quebec and interest rates remain low," said Cooper.
